findings.headline: Wyre In Bloom funding audited with 'limited' assurance, with audit recommending that the administration of grant funding be documented
findings.detail: Internal audit gave Wyre In Bloom a 'limited' opinion with three priority-level weaknesses. These concern undocumented funding administration, missing supporting files for each recipient, and the lack of grant applications, supplier invoices and meeting attendance evidence. A follow-up review was in progress at the time of the update.
findings.matters: Small council grants without documented supporting evidence are a recurring audit finding, and other councils administering community funding can check their own files against the same four categories of evidence.
findings.figures: 0 priority 1, 3 priority 2 recommendations; 'limited' assurance opinion
findings.quote: The procedure and processes used in the administration of the funding issued required documenting;

findings.headline: Procurement waiver register to be presented to the Audit and Standards Committee annually from June 2027, as reliance on waivers is expected to rise toward reorganisation
findings.detail: The paper states that waivers are permitted under the Contract Procedure Rules, and that there is concern that reliance on exemptions and waivers could increase as the council moves toward LGR. The action is to present a register of approved waivers, their rationale, values and trends to the committee, and the procurement waiver register will be included in the 2026/27 Annual Internal Audit Opinion.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare how waiver volumes and values are reported to members as the reorganisation date approaches, since waivers are a common route around competitive procurement in this period.
findings.figures: no waiver values are given in this paper; reporting date June 2027
findings.quote: there is concern that reliance on exemptions / waivers could increase

findings.headline: Council Plan projects to be reviewed for delivery before Local Government Reorganisation, with vesting day on 1 April 2028
findings.detail: The Annual Governance Statement action plan identifies a risk that future government spending controls, linked to a 'minded to' decision and any subsequent Section 24 notice, could restrict the council's ability to approve or progress new projects. The action is to identify the projects critical to delivery before reorganisation, with the Council Plan refresh going to Full Council on 26 November 2026.
findings.matters: A council in the reorganisation process reviewing its capital pipeline ahead of possible spending restrictions is a situation finance directors at other councils facing LGR will recognise and may be preparing for.
findings.figures: vesting day 1 April 2028; Council Plan refresh period April 2026 to October 2027; Full Council date 26 November 2026
findings.quote: This may result in delays to planned investments and impact the delivery of some corporate priorities.

findings.headline: Our Future Coast flood and coastal resilience project awarded £6,338,000 over five years from the Environment Agency's FCRIP programme, ending 31 March 2027
findings.detail: Wyre is one of 25 local areas funded from the £150 million Flood and Coastal Resilience Innovation Programme. The project is governed by a stakeholder board, and the paper states that the scheme was on track at the time of the update. The paper's text gives the completion date as 31 March 2026 in one place, and as 31 March 2027 elsewhere.
findings.matters: A £6,338,000 external grant ends on a fixed date, so its delivery and spend profile determines whether the council must fund any remaining work itself, a point finance directors on similar grant-funded programmes would track.
findings.figures: £6,338,000 total award over 5 years; £150 million FCRIP programme total; 25 local areas; end date 31 March 2027
findings.quote: awarded funding over 5 years, totalling £6,338,000, ending 31 March 2027.

findings.headline: Promenade widening at Cleveleys added by contract variation at £4,419,367, with completion scheduled for July 2027
findings.detail: The original Beach Management Scheme was completed on 21 April 2026. Savings from that scheme's project risk management and other efficiencies were used to agree a variation for the Cleveleys promenade widening. Construction is due to start on 9 November 2026, and a risk register was compiled on 6 October 2026, with monthly board meetings from 3 November 2026.
findings.matters: The council has used savings from a completed capital scheme to fund a further £4,419,367 of works under the same contract, a route other councils with coastal or similar schemes may compare against their own variation rules.
findings.figures: £4,419,367 variation value; construction start 9 November 2026; completion by July 2027
findings.quote: a variation to the original contract was agreed, allowing additional work on the widening of the promenade at Cleveleys costing £4,419,367 to be completed.

findings.headline: Cottam Hall Pavilion refurbishment completed on 30 March 2026 at a final cost of £1,033,332, against an original £618,000 allocation
findings.detail: The original £618,000 UKSPF allocation was spent by the 31 March 2025 deadline, but the project ran on to 30 March 2026. A further £250,000 allocation was approved on 9 January 2025. Internal audit gave the project a 'limited' assurance opinion and found no dedicated project manager, no full building survey, and a budget not based on technical designs. An HSE improvement notice also delayed construction.
findings.matters: A grant-funded capital scheme exceeded its budget by £165,332 and missed its funding deadline, and the paper attributes this to project governance and survey gaps that other councils running similar refurbishments could check against their own processes.
findings.figures: £618,000 original allocation; £250,000 further allocation approved 9 January 2025; £1,033,332 final cost; £165,332 overspend; UKSPF funding allocation £3,949,132
findings.quote: the project was not completed until the 30 March 2026 at a final cost of £1,033,332, an overspend of £165,332.

findings.headline: Prior-year value for money recommendation on budget holder involvement in budget setting is reported as implemented in 2025/26
findings.detail: The council's response to the earlier observation says finance officers and budget managers work together on budget development and that a sign-off proforma will be used for the 2026/27 budget. The update status is recorded as implemented in 2025/26.
findings.matters: Budget ownership by service managers is a control finance directors at other councils often struggle to evidence, so a documented sign-off process is a concrete reference point.
findings.quote: Implemented in 2025/26

findings.headline: Scale fee for the 2025/26 audit is set at £161,561 plus VAT, against £157,161 in 2024/25, with a fee variation under consideration
findings.detail: KPMG says it is considering the impact of the land and buildings valuation problems on its audit fees, and is working with management ahead of the 2026/27 audit to address the valuation issues.
findings.matters: Additional fees from audit delay or valuation problems are a cost a finance director at another council would want to anticipate when reviewing audit contracts.
findings.figures: £161,561 plus VAT scale fee for 2025/26; £157,161 scale fee for 2024/25
findings.quote: Our scale fee for the 2025/26 audit, as set by PSAA is £161,561 plus VAT (£157,161 in 2024/25).

findings.headline: Auditor has identified no risks of a significant weakness in the council's value for money arrangements, with no significant weaknesses found in financial sustainability, governance, or economy, efficiency and effectiveness
findings.detail: KPMG's value for money commentary covers all three domains and records no significant weaknesses. It raises one performance improvement observation, on Cabinet review of the strategic risk register.
findings.matters: Clean value for money conclusions alongside a disclaimed accounts opinion show the council's arrangements are assessed separately from the accounts problems, which peers and lenders would read differently.
findings.quote: As noted on the right, we have identified no risks of a significant weakness in the Council’s arrangements to secure value for money.

findings.headline: Auditor reports that the risk on the post retirement benefit obligation valuation has decreased, with no material misstatement found in the LGPS figures of £93.5m liabilities and £128.9m assets
findings.detail: The auditor found the actuary independent and of appropriate expertise, and agreed the actuarial results and accounting treatment were reasonable. It noted that management assumptions were optimistic for CPI, though still within the auditor's reasonable range.
findings.matters: A pension valuation that passes audit with no material misstatement is a reference point for other councils with LGPS deficits or surpluses, which the paper notes are becoming more common.
findings.figures: £93.5m present value of defined benefit obligations; £128.9m fair value of plan assets; £37.0m asset ceiling impact
findings.quote: We completed our planned procedures, and we did not identify any material misstatements relating to this area.

findings.headline: Uncorrected audit misstatements of £582k are recorded against income, surplus for the year and total assets
findings.detail: The uncorrected misstatements table shows a £582k item against income, with the same £582k shown against surplus for the year and total assets. The table gives percentages alongside each line.
findings.matters: Uncorrected misstatements that flow through income and the surplus show the size of unresolved adjustments that finance teams would need to understand before accepting the reported result.
findings.figures: £582k income; £582k surplus for the year (shown as a reduction); £582k total assets (shown as a reduction); 0.84%; 3.3%; 0.23%
findings.quote: Income 582 0.84

findings.headline: Two investment property valuations tested by the auditor carry misstatements of £304k overstatement and £157k understatement, against a portfolio valued at £16.0m at 31 March 2025
findings.detail: Both misstatements arose because the valuer did not deduct purchasers' costs. The auditor says the first yield used sits below the valuer's own comparables, and the second yield was too high for the type of asset.
findings.matters: Valuation errors in a commercial investment portfolio show how an external valuer's assumptions can move reported asset values, which other councils with similar property holdings would want to test.
findings.figures: £304k overstatement; £157k understatement; £16.0m investment properties valued at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: an overstatement of £304k – arose due to the valuer not deducting

findings.headline: Split of usable and unusable reserves for 31 March 2026 and 31 March 2025 has not been audited
findings.detail: The auditor has determined there is insufficient time to obtain evidence over the split of usable and unusable reserves before the backstop. Any adjustment would have a consequential effect on net assets and the split between the two reserve types.
findings.matters: The usable reserves figure is what a council can actually draw on, so an unverified split affects how finance directors and lenders read the council's available cushion.
findings.quote: insufficient time to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the split of useable and unusable reserves

findings.headline: Auditor was unable to complete work on the land and buildings valuation, which KPMG attributes to the quality of the external valuer's work
findings.detail: KPMG stopped work on land and buildings early in the audit and will revisit next year when the council plans a full portfolio valuation. It found the valuer, Aspin & Company, had used outdated floor area information and that the Gross Internal Area data could not be agreed to floorplans.
findings.matters: Property carrying values underpin the balance sheet, and a finance director at another council would want to know how a valuer's data errors can block audit assurance on the asset base.
findings.quote: The quality of the valuation of land and buildings undertaken by the Council’s external valuer.

findings.headline: KPMG intends to issue a disclaimer of opinion on Wyre's 2025/26 financial statements as a whole, with the statutory backstop date of 31 January 2027 cited as the reason work could not be completed
findings.detail: The auditor says the rebuilding of assurance is not complete and that there is insufficient time before the backstop to obtain evidence over the reserves split, which it considers pervasive to the financial position. It is therefore intending to disclaim the whole opinion rather than specific balances.
findings.matters: A disclaimer on the full set of accounts means the council's financial position cannot be relied on by lenders or peers through the audit opinion, and the same backstop pressure applies to other councils rebuilding assurance.
findings.figures: statutory backstop date of 31 January 2027
findings.quote: we intend to issue a disclaimer of opinion on the financial statements as a whole.

findings.headline: Wyre's budgeted total expenditure per head of population for 2025/26 is £174.91, 6th highest in its comparator group
findings.detail: The council's 2025/26 benchmarking study compared costs and performance against similar councils across housing, transport, culture, environmental services, planning and central services. The study was submitted to the Corporate Management Team in March 2026, and directors were encouraged to use it in service planning.
findings.matters: Per-head spend ranked against comparator councils is the benchmark finance officers at other councils use when judging their own cost position.
findings.figures: £174.91 budgeted total expenditure per head of population 2025/26; 6th highest in comparator group
findings.quote: For example, the council’s budgeted total expenditure per head of population for 2025/26 is £174.91, positioning Wyre 6th highest in the comparator group.

findings.headline: Lancashire's four-unitary local government reorganisation decision withdrawn in October 2026, with a structured review expected by early 2027
findings.detail: The proposal would have placed Wyre in a Fylde Coast unitary council with Fylde Borough Council, Blackpool Borough Council and disaggregated parts of Lancashire County Council, with implementation originally expected from 1 April 2028. The paper says reorganisation has the potential to affect governance, financial planning, service delivery and future value-for-money considerations.
findings.matters: The council's future structure and the bodies that would absorb its finances are unresolved, which matters to lenders and to any council facing the same reorganisation.
findings.figures: Implementation originally expected 1 April 2028; review outcome expected early 2027
findings.quote: In October 2026, the government announced the above decision has been withdrawn and a structured approach to review will now take place with an outcome expected by early 2027.

findings.headline: Head of Internal Audit gives reasonable assurance for 2025/26, the same result as in 2024/25
findings.detail: The opinion covers the overall adequacy and effectiveness of governance, risk management and internal control arrangements. It is the same result as the previous year.
findings.matters: A repeated reasonable-assurance opinion is the internal control result a finance director compares year on year.
findings.quote: The Head of Internal Audit Opinion for 2025/26 was that of reasonable assurance on the overall adequacy and effectiveness of the council’s governance, risk management, and internal control arrangements.

findings.headline: Auditor raises a Performance Improvement Observation on Cabinet oversight and challenge of strategic risks
findings.detail: Cabinet undertakes a financial risk assessment during its annual approval of the MTFP in February, but the auditor has not seen evidence of effective challenge of the strategic risk register more widely during the year. The strategic risk register was not required to be reviewed as part of the November 2025 MTFP update.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council may review how financial risk sits within the wider strategic risk framework, which this observation addresses.
findings.quote: We have therefore raised a Performance Improvement Observation (PIO) in relation to the level of Cabinet oversight and challenge of strategic risks.

findings.headline: 2025/26 budget documented anticipated efficiency savings of £111,350, with no efficiency programme that sets a percentage target
findings.detail: The auditor notes there is not currently a specific efficiency programme that states a target as a percentage of the previous year's expenditure, with schemes to achieve it. Efficiencies achieved in year are reported in the budget papers and in the narrative in the Statement of Accounts.
findings.matters: Savings reporting without a percentage-target programme is a gap that other councils and lenders can check against their own efficiency plans.
findings.figures: £111,350 anticipated savings
findings.quote: we acknowledge that as part of the 2025/26 budget a document outlining efficiencies was presented which set out anticipated savings of £111,350.

findings.headline: 2026/27 capital programme increased from £18.196m to £25.205m at quarter 1
findings.detail: The increase is mostly funded from grants, contributions or capital receipts, with only £411k from revenue contributions. Capital budget managers expect the schemes to be delivered on budget and within the financial year.
findings.matters: A roughly 38% rise in the in-year capital programme, mostly grant and receipt funded, is the kind of change that affects borrowing needs and delivery risk for peers and lenders.
findings.figures: £18.196m original 2026/27 capital programme; £25.205m at quarter 1; £411k from revenue contributions
findings.quote: The original approved capital programme for 2026/27 of £18.196m was increased to £25.205m at quarter 1.

findings.headline: 2026/27 net revenue budget of £19,067k approved with no additional drawdown from reserves
findings.detail: The budget was approved by Cabinet on 11 February 2026 and by full Council on 5 March 2026. At quarter 1, reported to Cabinet on 2 September 2026, there were no forecast under- or overspends across the main service lines and the year-end forecast remained a breakeven position.
findings.matters: A balanced budget with no reserve support, confirmed at quarter 1, is the position a finance director or lender tests against the council's reserve base.
findings.figures: £19,067k net revenue budget 2026/27; £18,196k original capital programme 2026/27
findings.quote: The budget for 2026/27 assumes no additional drawdown from reserves to balance the budget.

findings.headline: £2,000k of 2024/25 underspend carried forward into 2025/26, with £884k outstanding at the mid-year review
findings.detail: The Audit and Standards Committee approved the carry-forward in July 2025. At the mid-year review in November 2025, £1,116k of the slippage had been spent and £884k remained outstanding, mainly on contingency budgets and local plan consultancy work.
findings.matters: Carry-forwards from one year's underspend into the next are how councils move spending between years, and the outstanding balance shows how much had not yet been used.
findings.figures: £2,000k slippage approved; £1,116k spent at mid-year review; £884k outstanding
findings.quote: Of the £2,000k slippage approved, £1,116k had been spent to the date of the mid-year review, and £884k remained outstanding

findings.headline: Total reserves increased from £207.9m to £226.4m, and earmarked reserves increased from £36.5m to £42m
findings.detail: Usable reserves at 31 March 2026 were £46.2m and unusable reserves were £180.1m. Earmarked reserves rose over the year to £42m. The auditor states there are no concerns regarding the council's reserves balances.
findings.matters: A rise in total and earmarked reserves at year end is the figure a lender or peer finance director checks against the drawdown plans in the same year.
findings.figures: £207.9m total reserves at 31 March 2025; £226.4m at 31 March 2026; £46.2m usable reserves; £180.1m unusable reserves; £36.5m earmarked reserves 2024/25; £42m earmarked reserves 2025/26
findings.quote: Total reserves increased from £207.9m at 31 March 2025 to £226.4m at 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: Outturn for 2025/26 of £21,726k against a revised budget of £22,753k
findings.detail: The original 2025/26 budget of £20,531k was planned to break even with £1,030k drawn from earmarked reserves. The mid-year revised budget of £22,753k assumed £2,173k of drawdown (£473k earmarked and £1,700k general fund), after £2,000k of 2024/25 underspends were carried forward. The £1,981k favourable variance in the budget equalisation reserve was mostly from a £1,121k increase in waste collection grant income.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare the planned reserve drawdown with the outturn, and the grant-driven favourable variance shows how one income line changed the year-end result.
findings.figures: £20,531k original budget; £22,753k revised budget; £2,173k revised drawdown; £21,726k outturn; £1,981k favourable variance; £1,121k waste collection grant increase
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026, the outturn position was £21,726k vs. the revised budget of £22,753k following the mid-year review in November 2025.

findings.headline: Auditor's Annual Report issued before the auditor has reached conclusions on the 2025-26 financial statements and other information
findings.detail: The Code of Audit Practice requires the report by 30 November, so the auditor issued it before finishing work on the financial statements and other information. The auditor also cannot yet confirm it has concluded its Whole of Government Accounts procedures, and it may still use other powers on the 2025-26 audit.
findings.matters: The statements audit opinion is outstanding, so a reader relying on the 2025-26 accounts is working before the auditor's opinion is available.
findings.figures: Report deadline: 30 November
findings.quote: Consequently, we have not reached our conclusions in respect of these areas.

findings.headline: Auditor identifies no significant weaknesses in Wyre's arrangements for economy, efficiency and effectiveness in 2025-26
findings.detail: The auditor reports no significant risks and no actual significant weaknesses under each of the three value-for-money criteria: financial sustainability, governance, and improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness. The conclusions cover the 2025-26 year.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender, reads the value-for-money conclusion as the auditor's independent view of whether the council's financial arrangements are sound.
findings.quote: We identified no significant weaknesses in respect of the arrangements the Council has put in place to secure economy, efficiency, and effectiveness in the use of its resources.

findings.headline: Wyre reports its draft 2025/26 accounts were agreed by the S.151 Officer and published by 30 June 2026
findings.detail: The paper says the deadline was achieved, with draft accounts agreed by the S.151 Officer and published on the council's website by 30 June 2026. The same paragraph gives the deadline as 31 May 2026, so the two dates in the paper do not line up on their face. The paper also says the council must approve and publish the final Statement of Accounts by 31 January 2027, and this committee meets on 17 November 2026.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare the draft publication date and the stated deadline against their own timetable, though the paper's own dates need checking.
findings.figures: 31 May 2026 (deadline); 30 June 2026 (draft published); 31 January 2027 (approval deadline); 17 November 2026 (committee date)
findings.quote: This deadline has been achieved with the draft accounts being agreed by the S.151 Officer

findings.headline: Wyre says it is likely to receive disclaimed audit opinions on its accounts for at least another year
findings.detail: The paper states the council is likely to be subject to disclaimed opinions for at least another year. It says post-audit sign-off for the 2025/26 accounts will follow the same arrangements.
findings.matters: A run of disclaimed opinions would mean the council's audited position stays unverified for multiple years, which affects how lenders and other councils read its accounts.
findings.figures: at least another year; 2025/26 accounts; disclaimed opinions
findings.quote: the council is likely to be subject to disclaimed opinions on the accounts for at least another year.

findings.headline: Wyre's 2024/25 accounts were signed off under the backstop arrangements in February 2026 with a disclaimed opinion
findings.detail: The paper says the 2024/25 accounts were signed off under the 'backstop' arrangements, which it links to sector-wide audit delays. It describes the disclaimed opinion as a standard part of those arrangements.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means the auditor could not form a view on the accounts, which lenders and peer finance directors will read as a material audit outcome.
findings.figures: 2024/25 accounts; February 2026; disclaimed opinion
findings.quote: ‘backstop’ arrangements in February 2026, with a disclaimed opinion.

findings.headline: No internal audit follow-ups in 2025/26 or 2026/27 to date met the committee's criteria for requiring a senior officer to attend.
findings.detail: The Audit Charter requires a Service Manager or Senior Leadership Team member to attend the committee where an audit report receives a limited or minimal/no assurance opinion and the opinion is unchanged after two follow-ups. The paper says no follow-ups reached that threshold in the two years cited.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders look at whether internal audit weaknesses are being resolved, and this shows no audit reports reached the escalation threshold in the period.
findings.figures: 2025/26 and 2026/27 to date; two follow-ups as the escalation trigger
findings.quote: It should be noted that during 2025/26 and 2026/27 to date there were no follow ups meeting this criteria.

findings.headline: External audit's Annual ISA 260 Report for the year ended 31 March 2025 identified no significant weaknesses in the council's value for money arrangements.
findings.detail: The paper says the report was last presented to the committee on 24 February 2026. It relates to the council's value for money arrangements, which the committee scores 3.0 out of 5 as 'Established'.
findings.matters: A clean value for money finding from external audit is a specific assurance a finance director or lender would weigh when judging the council's governance of resources.
findings.figures: year ended 31 March 2025; value for money score 3.0 out of 5
findings.quote: which identified no significant weaknesses in respect of the arrangements.

findings.headline: The committee's self-assessment against the CIPFA 2026 maturity model gives an overall score of 4.1 'Advanced'.
findings.detail: The overall score is an average across all statements, on a scale of 1 to 5. The paper places 4.1 in the 'Advanced' band, which runs from 3.9 to under 4.7. The paper says maturity levels may fluctuate after a significant change in committee membership.
findings.matters: Peer councils using the same CIPFA model can compare their own self-assessment scores directly against this one.
findings.figures: 4.1 out of 5 overall; 'Advanced' band 3.9 to under 4.7
findings.quote: Overall maturity assessment 4.1 Advanced

findings.headline: Further committee training is deferred until after the May 2027 local elections, with the training date given as June 2027.
findings.detail: Committee members requested additional training, but the paper says it will be arranged after the election because membership may change. The paper's knowledge assessment for members is scored 3 out of 5.
findings.matters: A council that defers member training across an election period leaves a gap in committee knowledge that a lender or peer council would want to know about.
findings.figures: training to be arranged June 2027; local elections May 2027; knowledge score 3 out of 5
findings.quote: further training will be arranged after the election.

findings.headline: The Audit and Standards Committee has 12 elected members and one independent member, against the CIPFA 2026 recommended committee size of 8 members.
findings.detail: The paper records that the committee is combined with Standards and that its membership exceeds the recommended limit. It also records one independent member, where the CIPFA statement calls for at least two. The paper notes that the committee's knowledge requirements were identified as needing expansion in the November 2025 self-assessment.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council comparing audit committee arrangements against the same CIPFA 2026 position statement would see where Wyre's composition departs from it.
findings.figures: 12 elected members; one independent member; recommended limit of 8 members
findings.quote: The membership of the committee currently comprises of 12 elected members, plus one independent member.

findings.headline: The register records potential litigation and remediation costs from PFOA contamination in the Hillhouse Technology Enterprise Zone, with no sum stated.
findings.detail: The register says the council faces the risk of failing to fulfil its statutory duties to investigate and remediate contaminated land. It also says DEFRA has approved funding for Phase 4 of the Environment Agency's Part 2A investigation.
findings.matters: An unquantified contingent liability from contamination, alongside external funding for the investigation, is a pattern other councils dealing with legacy contamination would compare.
findings.figures: None stated for potential liability or remediation cost
findings.quote: Potential litigation from residents for alleged negligence or personal injury, as well as significant remediation costs / conveyancing loss.

findings.headline: The 2025/26 pay award is agreed at 3.2%, with nothing agreed beyond the current year.
findings.detail: The register notes that inflation was 3.0% in January 2026, above the Bank of England's 2% target but declining. The MTFP therefore carries pay assumptions only to the end of the current year.
findings.matters: An unagreed pay award beyond the current year is an open cost item in any multi-year budget, and finance directors at peers face the same uncertainty.
findings.figures: 3.2% (2025/26 pay award); 3.0% (inflation, Jan 26); 2% (Bank of England target)
findings.quote: The pay award for 2025/26 is now agreed at 3.2% but nothing beyond the current year has been agreed.

findings.headline: A staffing capacity provision of £318,000 has been included in the 26/27 budget, funded from reduced pension contributions.
findings.detail: The register says the provision is ongoing and that CMT will be able to draw on it to fund agreed priority roles.
findings.matters: Funding staff capacity from reduced pension contributions is a specific budget mechanism other councils may consider when managing workforce costs.
findings.figures: £318,000 (ongoing staffing capacity provision in 26/27 budget)
findings.quote: A staffing capacity provision, funded from reduced pension contributions has been included in the 26/27 budget (ongoing) commencing at £318,000.

findings.headline: The register says the efficiencies section of the MTFP still needs further development, including involvement from the Transformation Board.
findings.detail: The register says the efficiencies presentation was discussed at CMT. It also notes that a secondment has ended and that the Transformation Director prioritised asset and climate change work over the Transformation Board's list.
findings.matters: A savings programme still in development this late in the planning cycle is a signal finance directors check when judging whether efficiency targets are credible.
findings.figures: None stated
findings.quote: Efficiencies presentation discussed at CMT. Further development required including involvement from the Transformation Board.

findings.headline: The register says the Marine Hall Theatre's services are subsidised by the council, with the Waterfront bar project to be delivered by April 2027.
findings.detail: The register says the Marine Hall, Transformation and Estates teams will deliver the Waterfront project by April 2027, while the recorded action due date is 31/03/2028. The paper says the decision to keep Marine Hall management in-house followed the contingency options for an operator not being appointed by April 2026.
findings.matters: Ongoing subsidy for a council-run venue, and a decision to keep it in-house rather than contract it out, is a cost choice other councils weighing similar venues will compare.
findings.figures: Residual risk score 6 (inherent 9, target 4); action due 31/03/2028; Waterfront project target April 2027
findings.quote: The services operated from the theatre are subsidised by the council.

findings.headline: A multi-year settlement covering 2026/27 to 2028/29 has now been received.
findings.detail: The register says the settlement provides greater certainty over funding. LG Futures modelling has been procured to assess the impact of the Fair Funding Review 2.0.
findings.matters: A three-year settlement, rather than a single year, lets finance directors plan multi-year budgets with more confidence in central funding.
findings.figures: 2026/27 to 2028/29 (three-year settlement period)
findings.quote: Multi-year settlement now received covering 26/27 to 28/29.

findings.headline: The LGR pause announced 7 September 2026 has removed the MTFP's assumed move to a new unitary in April 2028.
findings.detail: The register says the MTFP previously indicated a strong and stable financial position moving to a new unitary in April 2028. It also says the pause may give more time to deliver transformation projects and cashable savings before any LGR restart.
findings.matters: Other councils planning for reorganisation face the same question of whether a stable MTFP assumes a structure that may not arrive.
findings.figures: 7 September 2026 (LGR pause announced); April 2028 (previously assumed unitary date)
findings.quote: following the LGR pause announced 7 September 2026, all certainty over the timing and inevitability of LGR has disappeared.

findings.headline: The register records pressure on reserves in the final two years of the MTFP, which 'would need to be addressed'.
findings.detail: The MTFP is being recast to include recent approvals and potential further investment projects. The register says the Autumn budget on 28 October 2026 may indicate changes to the indicative 2027/28 settlement.
findings.matters: Reserves that fall in the last years of a plan with no agreed fix are a direct signal of future financial sustainability for finance directors and lenders.
findings.figures: Autumn budget on 28 October 2026; MTFP final two years (period not quantified in the paper)
findings.quote: Pressure on reserves is concerning in the final two years of the MTFP and would need to be addressed.

findings.headline: Based on current spending, the register estimates a funding gap of £2.2m in 2026/27, rising to £4.7m in 2030/31.
findings.detail: The register says a renewed focus on savings is advisable now that LGR is delayed, and that a small number of potentially high-cost areas require monitoring. A multi-year settlement is noted as providing greater certainty.
findings.matters: A council publishing a specific gap for each year of its MTFP gives lenders and peers a concrete measure of the savings still to be found.
findings.figures: £2.2m (2026/27 funding gap); £4.7m (2030/31 funding gap)
findings.quote: Based on current spending, the estimated funding gap in 2026/27 is £2.2m, rising to £4.7m in 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: Printed minutes 29092026 1800 Audit and Standards Committee
findings.headline: KPMG could not previously collect data to test income from non-domestic rates because of the previous auditor's approach and a lack of available reports.
findings.detail: The paper, referring to page 14 of the agenda pack, says KPMG had been unable to collect data for tests on non-domestic rates income in prior audits. The cause is given as the previous auditor's approach and a lack of available reports.
findings.matters: Gaps in testing of a major income stream are a specific audit limitation that a finance officer at another council, or a lender reviewing assurance over income, would want to know about.
findings.quote: KPMG had previously been unable to collect data to undertake tests around income from non-domestic rates because of previous auditor’s approach and lack of reports available.

findings.paper_title: Printed minutes 29092026 1800 Audit and Standards Committee
findings.headline: KPMG's draft external audit plan for the year ended 31 March 2026 is intended to rebuild assurance towards an unqualified audit opinion, with property and equipment identified as the main challenge.
findings.detail: KPMG presented the draft plan and strategy and pointed to page 12-13 of the agenda pack for its risk assessment and material misstatements. Officers said the main challenge to the clean audit opinion involves the council's property and equipment, and KPMG is confident plans are in place to deal with this in next year's audit. Members noted the draft plan.
findings.matters: A council working to recover an unqualified opinion after audit problems gives a clear signal to lenders and peers about the status of assurance over fixed assets, a common pressure for councils.
findings.figures: year ended 31 March 2026
findings.quote: Officers highlighted that the main challenge to the clean audit opinion involved the council’s property and equipment

findings.paper_title: Printed minutes 29092026 1800 Audit and Standards Committee
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves (non-ring-fenced) could be less than £14 million as of 1 April 2029, compared with £33.5 million as of 1 April 2026.
findings.detail: The forecast is based on known requirements and Council Plan investment projects not yet formally approved. The paper says £3.6 million has been approved for the Investment Projects Reserve before 31 March 2028, comprising £2 million from the Leisure Management Reserve and £1.5 million from the Asset Management and Maintenance Reserve. It also says £4.4 million is already profiled in the MTFP for vehicles, including refuse collection vehicles in 2027/28. The MTFP report for Cabinet in November 2026 is to give the latest forecast.
findings.matters: The fall in unrestricted reserve headroom from the paper's figures is a funding position that finance directors and lenders would track against the council's capacity to absorb future pressures.
findings.figures: £33.5 million at 1 April 2026; less than £14 million at 1 April 2029; £3.6 million approved for Investment Projects Reserve before 31 March 2028; £2 million from Leisure Management Reserve; £1.5 million from Asset Management and Maintenance Reserve; £4.4 million profiled for vehicles in the MTFP
findings.quote: Earmarked Reserves (non-ring-fenced) could be less than £14 million as of 1 April 2029 compared to £33.5 million as of 1 April 2026.

findings.paper_title: Printed minutes 29092026 1800 Audit and Standards Committee
findings.headline: Wyre reports a £66,000 overspend in 2025/26, which officers attribute to water invoices for 2024/25 being billed in 2025/26 after a supplier change.
findings.detail: Members had asked why an overspend was reported when savings were expected after a water-cost audit. The Section 151 Officer said ledger review showed rebilling of 2024/25 invoices processed in 2025/26, understating 2024/25 costs and in some cases billing two years of water in 2025/26. The council has since moved to suppliers with a managed bill service and is increasing automated meter readings.
findings.matters: A finance director elsewhere can compare this billing-timing explanation and the supplier and metering response against utility cost overspends in their own accounts.
findings.figures: £66,000 overspend in 2025/26
findings.quote: an overspend of £66,000 was reported in 2025/26

findings.headline: One related party transaction was omitted from the draft financial statement disclosures.
findings.detail: KPMG reports this as a disclosure misstatement, with no effect on the amounts in the accounts. It is listed alongside the other control and disclosure findings in the audit summary.
findings.matters: Related party disclosure omissions are a governance point finance officers at other councils will check in their own year-end processes.
findings.figures: 1 related party disclosure misstatement
findings.quote: One related party transaction omitted from disclosures.

findings.headline: KPMG's 2025/26 scale fee is £161,561 plus VAT, up from £157,161 in 2024/25, with a fee variation under consideration.
findings.detail: KPMG says it is still considering the impact of the land and buildings valuation problems on its audit fee. It is working with management to address the issue before the 2026/27 audit.
findings.matters: Audit fee variations linked to valuation quality are a cost pressure other councils with similar valuation issues may face.
findings.quote: Our scale fee for the 2025/26 audit, as set by PSAA is £161,561 plus VAT (£157,161 in 2024/25).

findings.headline: Cabinet now receives quarterly Strategic Risk Register reports, in response to a prior value for money observation on Cabinet's challenge of risk in financial planning.
findings.detail: KPMG had found no evidence that Cabinet challenged the strategic risk register during the year, and the November 2025 MTFP update did not require a review. The council's response says the Q2 report now coincides with the mid-year MTFP update.
findings.matters: Linking the risk register to the MTFP cycle is a governance change finance directors at other councils can compare with their own reporting timetables.
findings.quote: Cabinet now receive quarterly reports on the Strategic Risk Register for consideration and challenge.

findings.headline: The council reports the prior-year value-for-money observation on budget-holder involvement in budget setting as implemented in 2025/26.
findings.detail: KPMG's prior-year observation found meetings between budget holders and finance business partners were not logged and actions not tracked. The council's update, which KPMG reproduces, says a proforma for proposed changes was introduced for the 2026/27 budget setting process.
findings.matters: Logging budget-holder engagement in the budget process is a practical control other councils can adopt, and this shows the council closing a prior observation.
findings.quote: Implemented in 2025/26

findings.headline: KPMG identifies no risks of significant weakness in Wyre's value for money arrangements across all three domains.
findings.detail: KPMG assessed financial sustainability, governance, and improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness as having no significant risks and no significant weaknesses. It records one performance improvement observation, which is not linked to a significant weakness.
findings.matters: A clean value for money conclusion alongside a disclaimed opinion is a combination other councils will want to see, as it separates the accounts problem from arrangements.
findings.quote: As noted on the right, we have identified no risks of a significant weakness in the Council’s arrangements to secure value for money.

findings.headline: KPMG reports no material misstatements in the pension valuation, with LGPS gross assets of £128.9m and gross liabilities of £93.5m.
findings.detail: KPMG assessed the actuary's assumptions as optimistic but within its reasonable range and reports that the actuarial results and accounting treatment are reasonable. Amendments were required to pension disclosures in the draft accounts.
findings.matters: The pension valuation finding is one of the three areas where KPMG completed its procedures without material misstatement, which is relevant to peers managing similar LGPS balances.
findings.figures: LGPS gross assets £128.9m; LGPS gross liabilities £93.5m; asset ceiling impact £37.0m
findings.quote: Our audit procedures did not identify any material misstatements.

findings.headline: KPMG reports one significant control deficiency, four other control deficiencies and two prior-year deficiencies remediated.
findings.detail: The control deficiency counts sit alongside KPMG's findings on the valuation review controls and on the lack of enforced segregation of duties in manual journal posting. KPMG notes the segregation issue remains relevant from the prior year.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare the counts and the type of control gaps, such as valuation review and journal segregation, against their own audit findings.
findings.figures: 1 significant control deficiency; 4 other control deficiencies; 2 prior-year deficiencies remediated
findings.quote: Prior year control deficiencies remediated

findings.headline: KPMG cites the statutory backstop date of 31 January 2027 for the 2025/26 audit, after disclaimers for 2023/24 and 2024/25.
findings.detail: KPMG says the backstop leaves insufficient time to obtain evidence on the reserves split as at 31 March 2026 and 2025. It also records that the predecessor auditor issued disclaimers for earlier years, and that KPMG issued a disclaimer for 2023/24 on 27 February.
findings.matters: The backstop deadline determines whether a council can rebuild assurance in time, and the same deadline applies to every council with open legacy audits.
findings.figures: 31 January 2027 backstop date
findings.quote: due to the statutory backstop date of 31 January 2027

findings.headline: KPMG's testing of two investment properties found a £304k overstatement and a £157k understatement in their valuations.
findings.detail: In both cases the valuer did not deduct purchasers' costs. KPMG says the first valuation used a gross yield below the valuer's own comparables, and that the second used a yield too high for the asset type. Investment property was valued at £16.0m at 31 March 2025.
findings.matters: Yield and purchasers' cost assumptions in external valuations are a common source of misstatement, so peers using the same valuation approach may want to check their own figures.
findings.figures: £304k overstatement; £157k understatement; £16.0m investment property valued at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: an overstatement of £304k

findings.headline: KPMG has been unable to complete procedures on the land and buildings valuation prepared by Aspin & Company, citing gross internal area data that does not agree to floorplans.
findings.detail: KPMG stopped work on the land and buildings valuation early in the year-end audit and agreed with management to revisit it when the council plans a full portfolio valuation. It reports that a sample of GIA figures, once used in the valuation calculation, gave a material variance in the overall valuation of the asset.
findings.matters: Valuation data quality on a rolling five-year revaluation model is a risk other councils using external valuers will recognise, and it delays the rebuilding of assurance.
findings.quote: The GIA data per the valuation reports could not be agreed to floorplans provided to us by the audited entity.

findings.headline: KPMG intends to issue a disclaimer of opinion on Wyre's 2025/26 financial statements as a whole.
findings.detail: KPMG states that it could not obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the split of usable and unusable reserves and over several other areas before the statutory backstop. It attributes the pervasiveness of these matters to the disclaimer.
findings.matters: A disclaimer on the full set of accounts is a concrete audit outcome that other councils with unresolved valuation or reserves work will want to compare against.
findings.quote: As a result of the pervasiveness of the above, we intend to issue a disclaimer of opinion on the financial statements as a whole.

findings.headline: The Chief Executive attended the committee's meeting on 19/05/26, where the Annual Opinion, Internal Audit Effectiveness and the Annual Governance Statement were presented, and will be asked to attend future meetings.
findings.detail: The action plan had committed to inviting the Chief Executive to the meeting that considers the Annual Opinion, Internal Audit Effectiveness and the Annual Governance Statement, to strengthen reporting to those in leadership roles. The status records attendance on 19/05/26 and an ongoing request to attend.
findings.matters: Chief Executive attendance at the audit committee for the annual governance statement is a change in how the council's top officer is involved in assurance reporting, which a finance director elsewhere may compare with their own arrangements.
findings.quote: The Chief Executive attended the meeting on

findings.detail: The action plan says the committee's knowledge requirements need expanding and that further training was not yet provided. It states that membership may change at the May 2027 elections, so training is deferred to June 2027 and a skills register will then be compiled.
findings.matters: Deferring member training on audit committee knowledge until after an election is a timing decision that peers and lenders reviewing governance capacity may want to note.
findings.figures: May 2027, June 2027
findings.quote: the local elections in May 2027 may

findings.headline: The committee's terms of reference were updated on 24/02/26 to match the example terms of reference in the CIPFA guidance, as the action plan set out.
findings.detail: The action plan committed to updating the terms of reference at the February 2026 review. The status column records that they were updated and approved by the committee on 24/02/26.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare this terms of reference change against the CIPFA example when reviewing their own audit committee.
findings.quote: TOR updated 24/02/26

findings.paper_title: Annual Review of Audit and Standards Committees Performance
findings.headline: Further CIPFA training for audit committee members is scheduled for June 2027, after the May 2027 local elections.
findings.detail: The self-assessment identified additional member training as needed. The council has deferred it because the elections may change the committee's membership.
findings.matters: Finance officers at other councils may face the same timing question when member changes follow an election and training needs to be scheduled around them.
findings.quote: further training by CIPFA will be arranged in June 2027.

findings.paper_title: Annual Review of Audit and Standards Committees Performance
findings.headline: CIPFA issued a revised Position Statement on audit committees in October 2026, replacing the 2022 edition.
findings.detail: The revised statement sets out CIPFA's view of audit committee practice that UK local government bodies should adopt. Companion guidance was also updated to the 2026 edition, and the council's self-assessment is measured against it.
findings.matters: Every council's audit committee is measured against the same revised statement, so peers' assessments and any changes they make will be comparable.
findings.quote: In October 2026, CIPFA issued a revised Position Statement: Audit Committees in Local Authorities 2026, replacing the 2022 edition.

findings.paper_title: Annual Review of Audit and Standards Committees Performance
findings.headline: Wyre's Audit and Standards Committee scores 4.1 on CIPFA's 2026 maturity model, in the Advanced band.
findings.detail: The Audit and Risk Manager completed the self-assessment, which the Section 151 Officer and Monitoring Officer reviewed. The paper's scoring table places 3.9 to below 4.7 in the Advanced band.
findings.matters: Finance directors at other councils can compare this score against their own audit committee self-assessments under the same new CIPFA tool.

findings.quote: Based on the completion of this assessment the overall maturity score of 4.1 Advanced was calculated.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Council Plan Monitoring Quarter 2 2026/27
findings.headline: Building Pride campaign launch slipped to Quarter 3 as Communications and Visitor Economy capacity remains reduced
findings.detail: The paper says the branded campaign was planned for Quarter 2 but has slipped, and that the team's reduced capacity is affecting milestone delivery. Recruitment to the remaining vacant post is an action for Quarter 3.
findings.matters: A vacancy delaying a council's own campaign and delivery milestones is a staffing signal finance directors and HR leads in similar small comms teams will recognise.
findings.quote: There continues to be reduced capacity in the Communications and Visitor Economy team that we are managing, while maintaining our focus on quality internal and external comms.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Council Plan Monitoring Quarter 2 2026/27
findings.headline: Leisure centre memberships at 8,775 and up over 20%, while visitor numbers of 274,468 were below a 282,000 target after temporary closures
findings.detail: The paper attributes lower visitor numbers to temporary closures and disruption at several Health and Fitness centres during improvement works. It reports membership growth and expects usage to rise as the improved facilities become fully operational.
findings.matters: Membership growth set against closure-driven visitor losses is a pattern that bears on the income lines of council leisure services, which peer finance officers managing similar facilities will compare.
findings.figures: 8,775 total memberships; memberships increased by over 20%; 274,468 visitors against a 282,000 target
findings.quote: memberships have increased by over 20% and usage is expected to continue increasing as the improved facilities become fully operational.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Council Plan Monitoring Quarter 2 2026/27
findings.headline: Wyre Local Plan review rated Red, with the current timetable no longer achievable under the new plan-making system
findings.detail: Officers report that new Local Plan regulations in force from March 2026 and a revised National Planning Policy Framework published in August 2026 require a revised timetable. Updates to the Strategic Flood Risk Assessment Level 1 and the Local Plan Viability Assessment have been commissioned, and infrastructure and site-specific issues may affect potential site allocations.
findings.matters: A council that cannot hold its plan-making timetable carries delay risk for site allocations and development land, which lenders and peer councils watch in planning-led growth areas.
findings.quote: The transition to the new Local Plan system will require a revised timetable to be prepared as the current timetable can no longer be achieved.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Council Plan Monitoring Quarter 2 2026/27
findings.headline: Government announced a pause to its rapid review of local government reorganisation towards the end of Quarter 2
findings.detail: The paper says councils were advised to plan for 2027 local elections on current boundaries, extending anticipated timescales. Wyre expects to continue beyond 31 March 2028 and says the pause will require a further review of financial planning and corporate priorities. Staff and member arrangements await guidance from MHCLG.
findings.matters: A pause to Lancashire's unitary reorganisation shifts when the county's councils will restructure their finances and assets, which is a timetable finance directors across the county will be planning around.
findings.figures: Expected continuation beyond 31 March 2028; MHCLG update expected by end of October
findings.quote: The pause creates delay and potential rework.It will require a further review of financial planning and corporate priorities.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Council Plan Monitoring Quarter 2 2026/27
findings.headline: Percentage of duties owed where homelessness was prevented at 63% against a 78% target
findings.detail: The paper cites a continuing shortage of affordable private rented and social housing, and says the Renters' Rights Act has reduced the number of landlords in the private rented sector. Performance improved from Quarter 1, and approval has been secured to recruit two extra Housing Options Advisors.
findings.matters: Homelessness demand and temporary accommodation are budget pressures that finance directors plan for, and the paper links the shortfall to housing supply and a national change in private renting rules.
findings.figures: 63% actual against a 78% target; 105 of 168 cases successful; 62 of 80 prevention cases (78%); 43 of 88 relief cases (49%)
findings.quote: Performance remains below target due to a continuing shortage of affordable private rented and social housing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Council Plan Monitoring Quarter 2 2026/27
findings.headline: Holiday activities places at 1,404 against a 1,650 target after Lancashire County Council reduced its funding
findings.detail: The paper says Lancashire County Council reduced its 2026/27 funding while eligibility and demand rose. Provider costs for staffing, venue hire and food also increased, so fewer places were available than planned. The council says it will maximise places within the funding it has.
findings.matters: A county grant cut passed through to a district service, combined with cost inflation for providers, is a pattern finance officers at other district councils dependent on county funding will recognise.
findings.figures: 1,404 children engaged against a 1,650 target; county funding reduced by 7.5%
findings.quote: Funding provided by Lancashire County Council for 2026/27 was reduced by 7.5% at a time when more children were eligible and demand for places continued to increase.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Council Plan Monitoring Quarter 2 2026/27
findings.headline: Council tax collection at 53.8% at Quarter 2 against a 54.0% target
findings.detail: The paper describes the shortfall as a marginal reduction and links the lower in-year rate to cost-of-living pressure on some taxpayers' regular payment arrangements. Collection will be monitored against previous years and other Lancashire authorities in Quarters 3 and 4.
findings.matters: In-year council tax collection is a cash-flow indicator that finance directors and lenders track, and the paper ties the shortfall to household finances.
findings.figures: 53.8% actual; 54.0% target; reduction of 0.22%
findings.quote: A marginal reduction of 0.22%.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Council Plan Monitoring Quarter 2 2026/27
findings.headline: Business rates collection at 55.7% at the end of Quarter 2 against a 60.0% target, with approximately £934k unallocated at quarter end
findings.detail: The paper attributes most of the variance to a change in how schools' business rates are paid: responsibility moved from Lancashire County Council to the Department for Education. The payment was received, but later than in previous years, so it was not reflected in the quarter-end statistics.
findings.matters: A central-government change to how a major payer settles its bills shifted in-year collection figures, which finance officers here and at peer councils will need to explain to members.

findings.detail: The project was set up to explore buying retail and employment land to develop a local retail unit and commercial units for rental income. The paper says no further action is planned, though the project could move to development if an update is received.

findings.headline: Wyre's ESG investment protocol is recommended for formal adoption at Full Council on 26 November 2026
findings.detail: The finance team has piloted a protocol that considers Environmental, Social and Governance factors only after an investment meets minimum security and liquidity requirements. The recommendation is to adopt it formally through the mid-year Treasury Management report.

findings.paper_title: 20261105 T Mngt Questions and answers 2026-27 OS version for members new template
findings.headline: Interest received for 2025/26 reached an outturn of £1,949,000 against an original budget of £1,250,000
findings.detail: The Audit and Standards Committee extract reproduced in the paper records interest received of £2,265,130 in 2024/25 and a 2025/26 original budget of £1,250,000.
